2026 · Materials

Mineral foam and fibre: where the materials strategy stands

The current SeaBrick material is a light mineral-composite core inside a denser mineral shell, reinforced with short plant fibres. Here is the thinking, and the open questions.

A floating brick asks its material to do two jobs that pull in opposite directions. It must be light enough to provide useful buoyancy, and strong enough to carry the forces that pass between connected bricks when a platform flexes in a swell. Fibre composites solved the second job well. They were never going to solve the first on their own, and they brought the problem of water with them.

The strategy that emerged through 2026 separates the two jobs.

A light core and a dense shell

The core is a mineral foam: a low-density mineral composite that supplies most of the brick's buoyancy. The reference formulation uses lightweight glass particles in a magnesium-silicate binder; lighter versions that replace some of the solid with controlled air foam are being compared against it. The practical question is how light the cured core can be made before it loses strength, dimensional stability or resistance to water uptake.

The shell is a denser mineral layer around the core, with the most solid material concentrated where bricks grip one another. It protects the core, gives a hard surface at the joints and carries contact loads. A barrier coating goes over that.

The fibre is short, treated plant fibre mixed into the core: the thread that connects this strategy to the project's kelp and flax years. Fibre adds strength and reduces brittleness. Whether it keeps doing so through curing and long wet exposure depends on the chemistry around it, which is one of the things now being tested.

Why mineral

Mineral binders of this kind have a much lower emissions profile than Portland cement, they are not affected by seawater the way steel-reinforced concrete is, and they do not swell. Adding plant fibre to the mix lowers the carbon footprint further, and some of the reactive mineral content continues to absorb carbon dioxide over the life of the brick. We are careful not to claim more than that: the material should have far lower emissions than concrete, but whether a finished brick is fully carbon-negative is not yet established.

What is being tested next

The next round of work compares matched batches of the reference core and the air-foam hybrid against four questions:

  • Density, dry and conditioned, and how much it varies from batch to batch.
  • Water uptake under immersion, pressure and wet-dry cycling, especially after the surface has been deliberately damaged.
  • Shrinkage, fibre toughness and the bond between core and shell through curing and ageing.
  • Whether the mix can be placed and demoulded reliably from a two-part mould, producing one finished brick per cycle.

Buoyancy is assessed net of shell, coating, absorbed water and payload, not on the core alone. Until a full-size brick has been through this programme and marine exposure testing, the system is a research design, not a qualified product.

Where kelp and flax fit

The kelp composite and the flax and hemp work were stages of this research, and what they taught about fibre, binders, moisture and supply is built into the current approach. They are part of the history rather than the definition of the current system.
